Masking cannot manufacture the case either: SourceMask's @blank is 0x01, which matches neither `\w` nor `\s`, so the shadow never carries a word byte the source lacks. survivors.argument: Column 77 is the `1` inside the SECOND arm of capture1?: `match?({:&, _, [{:__block__, _, [1]}]}, a)`. That arm is not dead code. Sourceror parses with a literal_encoder, and the bare `&1` token is emitted by the parser as `{:&, meta, [1]}` with the integer NOT passed through the encoder (verified) — that is what the first arm catches. But when the placeholder is written so that `&` applies to a parenthesized integer, the integer DOES go through the encoder and the node becomes `{:&, meta, [{:__block__, meta2, [1]}]}` — exactly the second arm's shape. `&((&(1)) != "")` is valid, compiling Elixir: its plain (encoder-free) AST is identical to that of `&(&1 != "")` — `{:&,_,[{:!=,_,[{:&,_,[1]},""]}]}` — and it evaluates identically (both give ["a","b"] on "a,,b"). With the literal at 1, empty_filter_call?/1 returns true: check/2 emits the issue and fix_patches/2 rewrites to `String.split(",", trim: true)`. With it mutated to 0, neither arm of capture1? matches (first arm wants an unwrapped 1, second now wants 0), capture2?/empty1? are false too, so empty_filter_call?/1 returns false and BOTH check and fix go silent. Simulated the predicate on the real Sourceror-shaped AST: literal=1 -> true, literal=0 -> false. The triplet misses it because all six fixtures write the bare `&1` token, which only ever exercises the first arm. (The opposite direction — mutant fires where original doesn't — is indeed blocked by CompileError, since `&0` is not a legal capture index; but the forward direction above is a genuine separating input, so this is a GAP, not an equivalence.)

The extra index the mutant scans is `opener_at` itself, and locate/1 has already pattern-matched `{:ok, opener_at, ?{}`, so that byte is always `{`. What its handler does depends on the depth there, and the depth there is provably 0: SourceMask.enclosing_opener/2 walked the identical byte range with the identical +1/-1 arithmetic and HALTED at opener_at, which it only does at depth 0. (The same invariant makes entry_start's and enclosing_opener's depth sequences identical over the region — every opener inside it was seen at depth > 0, so entry_start's `max(_, 0)` never clamps.) So the extra step computes max(0-1,0) = 0, the reduce still ends with found = 0, and `found > 0` is still false: both take the `else` branch and return `opener_at + 1`. In the ordinary case the scan halts on a depth-0 comma before ever reaching opener_at, so the range end is not consulted at all. Confirmed: 0 differences over 785 generated shapes, including map-update forms and deep nesting.

That byte is `{` (locate/1 matched `{:ok, opener_at, ?{}`), and the `byte in [?(, ?[, ?{]` clause can never HALT, so the mutant and original can only differ in the FALL-THROUGH value: original returns depth d, mutant returns max(d-1,0). Those differ whenever d >= 1 (d == 1 flips the `found > 0` branch to the else arm; d >= 2 shifts entry_start down by one and misplaces the whole rewrite). So the real separating condition is `residual depth >= 1`, not the identity of the extra byte. That condition is unreachable: SourceMask.enclosing_opener/2 (lib/source_mask.ex:183) walked the identical shadow over the identical descending range from comma_at-1, its cond differs from entry_start/3's only in halting on a depth-0 opener versus clamping, and its FIRST halt was at opener_at — so no opener in (opener_at, comma_at) sat at depth 0, `depth - 1` and `max(depth - 1, 0)` coincide throughout, the two depth sequences are bit-identical, and the depth entering opener_at is 0 by enclosing_opener's own halt guard. This is a shadow-internal argument, so it holds even if mask/1 and the tokenizer disagree about what is code. If entry_start/3 instead halts on a comma, the extra index is never visited at all. Empirically: 0 differences and 0 fall-through depths != 0 over 18,390 generated sources (15,623 reaching locate/1's body, 1,979 via the comma-halt path), using a standalone re-implementation loading lib/source_mask.ex with Code.string_to_quoted(columns: true) in place of Sourceror.parse_string/1 (Sourceror passes the same columns: true and returns Code's error tuple unchanged).

survivors.argument: The guard separates a halt index from the fall-through depth, and the boundary value entry_start is unreachable for both. Halt case: halting at index == entry_start would mean the entry's very first byte is a code `:` immediately followed by whitespace; in Elixir a colon followed by whitespace is only ever a keyword-key terminator, and its key occupies at least one byte before it (mask/1 preserves byte counts, so `"a b":` and even `"":` still leave >= 2 bytes), while a bare `%{: ...` is rejected by the tokenizer as `unexpected token :` and never produces the keyword-list message. So the colon is always strictly right of entry_start. Fall-through case: the reduce returns the residual depth, and the scanned region is bracket-balanced (it is a suffix of the region enclosing_opener certified), so that depth is 0 — while entry_start >= 2 — and both `>=` and `>` reject alike. Confirmed: 0 differences over 785 generated shapes.

The guard separates a halt index from a fall-through depth, and the boundary value entry_start is unreachable on both. (a) Fall-through: the claim says the region is 'bracket-balanced' without proof. It follows from the backward walk — over [entry_start, comma_at-1] the entry_start/3 traversal ended at depth 0 with no clamping, so opener and closer counts are equal and every right-suffix has closers >= openers, which is exactly the statement that every left-prefix has openers >= closers; therefore key_colon/3's FORWARD walk never clamps either and its residual is exactly 0. Since entry_start >= opener_at + 1 >= 2 (opener_at >= 1 because byte_at(shadow, opener_at - 1) == ?% must have succeeded), 0 >= entry_start and 0 > entry_start are both false. (b) Halt at index == entry_start would require a code `:` followed by whitespace at the entry's very first byte, i.e. the literal `{:` or `,:` followed by space/tab/CR/LF. I tested this against Elixir 1.20.2 rather than reasoning about it: `%{: 1, "k" => 2}`, `%{a: 1,: 2, ...}` (with space, tab, LF and CRLF after the colon), `<<1,: 2>>`, `fn x,: y ->`, `[1,: 2]`, `f(1,: 2)` and `{1,: 2}` all fail with `unexpected token: ":"`, and `%{a: 1,:: 2, ...}` / `%{:: 1, ...}` fail with `syntax error before: '::'` — none carries the @message_fragment `unexpected expression after keyword list`, so locate/1 declines at the message check before entry_start/3 ever runs.
